2023_20_2023_troy_school_district_draft_.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC delivered its draft Report to the Board of Education for Troy School District covering the year ended June 30, 2023, dated October 3, 2023 and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager). It reports a clean audit process — no disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, and all identified misstatements corrected — plus recommendations and informational items on Michigan school funding. Most consequentially, 2022/2023 General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, leaving fund balance at approximately $32,620,000, or 17.2 percent of expenditures (about 8.9 weeks of operations) against a 20.30 percent statewide average.
2023_20_2023_troy_school_district_draft_.page:
**What it is**
Draft "Report to the Board of Education" from Plante & Moran, PLLC accompanying the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. Dated October 3, 2023; signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. Sections: Results of the Audit (pp. 3-6), Other Recommendations and Observations (pp. 7-8), Informational Items (pp. 9-19). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

**Audit results**
Engagement letter dated May 31, 2023; planning matters discussed at an August 4, 2023 meeting; audit report and management representation letter both dated October 3, 2023; a separate October 3, 2023 letter covers internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing under Government Auditing Standards. No new accounting policies were adopted in 2023. No difficulties, no disagreements with management, no consultations with other independent accountants; management corrected all accumulated misstatements. Most sensitive estimates were the district's shares of MPSERS net liabilities per GASB 68 and GASB 75.

| Estimate at June 30, 2023 | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| MPSERS net pension liability share | $340,447,659 |
| MPSERS net OPEB liability share | $19,240,985 |

**Other recommendations and observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1: group purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in aggregate must be capitalized; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum of three months' operating expenditures; the district should continue its spenddown plan with the Michigan Department of Education.
- Troy Career Center (MiWorks): the program director tracks expenditures manually in an Excel template serving as the subsidiary ledger, including the WIOA program tested in the single audit; automation or more frequent reconciliation recommended.
- Inflation Reduction Act (signed August 16, 2022; $369 billion over 10 years toward roughly 40 percent emissions reduction by 2030) offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option on qualifying capital projects such as electric vehicles and solar.

**Fund balance**
General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000 in 2022/2023, reducing fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023 — 17.2 percent of expenditures, about 8.9 weeks of operation. The statewide average at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent, roughly 10 weeks.

**State funding landscape**
The 2023/2024 target foundation allowance rose 5 percent, or $458 per pupil, to $9,608; 2022/2023 was $9,150 after a $450 increase. Cyber schools remain at $9,150. Pupil count stays 90 percent October 2023 / 10 percent February 2023, with a Section 29 two-year blend for declining-enrollment districts. State special education funding moved fully to Section 51 from Section 20, completing the Headlee Amendment funding shift. Other changes: a Section 31a At-Risk opportunity index, Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch, GSRP eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty, a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula, one-time mental health, school safety, and student loan repayment funding, and a 5 percent ISD operations increase. Federal pandemic education aid concludes September 30, 2024.

**MPSERS plan-level status (September 30, 2022)**
Net pension liability approximately $37.9 billion, up about 57 percent from $24.2 billion a year earlier; net OPEB liability approximately $2.1 billion, up about 40 percent from $1.5 billion. Driver: a 27.2 percent return for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**Other informational items**
GASB financial reporting model project (exposure draft June 2020, final standards targeted March 2024, governmental funds tentatively removed from scope in June 2023); a Revenue and Expense Recognition standard anticipated 2027; GASB 101 Compensated Absences effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 permitting transportation uses for millages approved after May 7, 2023, with separate accounting by authorization date; Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 superseding Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 for June 30, 2024 audits; arbitrage compliance at the five-year bond anniversary; cybersecurity risk and the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021; and real estate options via Plante Moran Cresa.
2023_20_2023_troy_school_district_draft_.verbose:
**Document identity and engagement terms**
A draft communication titled "Troy School District — Report to the Board of Education, June 30, 2023," issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 3, 2023. Every page is watermarked DRAFT and footed "Ver. 02/2023." The firm audited the basic financial statements of Troy School District (the "School District") as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023 and issued its audit report thereon dated October 3, 2023. The transmittal letter directs the Board to three sections: Results of the Audit (pages 3-6), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 7-8), and Informational Items (pages 9-19). It thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness, is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager, and states it is intended solely for the Board of Education and management.

Responsibilities were established in an engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, and the audit followed the scope and timing communicated at a planning meeting on August 4, 2023. Beyond U.S. generally accepted auditing standards, the audit was conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, which obligates the firm to communicate matters including compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; error or fraud; illegal acts; and significant internal control deficiencies. A separate letter dated October 3, 2023 addressed internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance.

**Significant audit findings**
No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies did not change during 2023; significant policies are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No transactions were entered into for which authoritative guidance or consensus is lacking, and no significant transactions were recognized in a period other than when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. As of June 30, 2023 those estimates were $340,447,659 (pension) and $19,240,985 (OPEB), based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services; the firm evaluated key factors and assumptions and found them reasonable relative to the financial statements as a whole. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered in performing or completing the audit; no disagreements with management arose; management corrected all accumulated known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones; there were no consultations with other independent accountants; and a management representation letter dated October 3, 2023 was obtained. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to its attention suggesting that other information was materially misstated or materially inconsistent with the financial statements.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the clarified guidance takes effect for the year ending June 30, 2024, and the district should align practices and written policies.

Food Service Fund fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the School District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan it entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

Troy Career Center (MiWorks) expenditure reporting is tracked manually: the program director enters all Troy Career Center federal and state expenditures into an Excel template that serves as the subsidiary ledger by program — including the WIOA program tested in the single audit — and shares it with the business office. The auditors encourage evaluating a more automated tracking process or, alternatively, more frequent reconciliation to reduce allocation errors.

The Inflation Reduction Act, signed into law August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over ten years for energy and climate projects aimed at reducing emissions approximately 40 percent by 2030. Its direct-payment option, in lieu of a nonrefundable tax credit, is available to tax-exempt entities including governmental entities, reimbursing part of the cost of qualifying capital improvements such as certain electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment (for example solar panels).

**Fund balance**
During the 2022/2023 school year, General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would equate to roughly 10 weeks of average operating costs. Troy's fund balance percentage is 17.2 percent, equal to approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

**School funding — new initiatives and state aid**
The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs plus substantial resources for new initiatives; the School Aid Bill for 2023/2024 was completed and signed into law. In 2022/2023 schools saw the largest per-pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995), with all districts except a few hold harmless districts funded at the $9,150 target foundation allowance and all districts receiving a $450 per-pupil increase. For 2023/2024 the target foundation allowance rose 5 percent, or $458 per pupil, to $9,608; hold harmless districts also receive the $458 increase, while cyber schools received no increase and remain at $9,150.

Other 2023/2024 provisions described: new funding for declining enrollment districts to smooth revenue decline; continuation of the blended pupil count at 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a two-year blend available to districts whose 2023 final membership count is lower than 2022, funded through Section 29 (calculated as the foundation allowance times the difference between a 50/50 blend of the 2022 and 2023 blended counts and the blended 2023 count); completion of the shift of state special education funding to Section 51 of the State Aid Act from Section 20, so that the Headlee Amendment obligation is met from the special education categorical rather than the foundation allowance; increased Great Start Readiness Program reimbursement at the target foundation allowance level with income eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty; increased Section 31a At-Risk funding using an opportunity index; revised Section 31d providing universal free breakfast and lunch, state funded and supplemental to the federal Child Nutrition Cluster; additional transportation funding using a riders-per-square-mile formula; one-time funding for student mental health and school safety; a one-time student loan repayment program for employees working directly with students; increased retirement system contributions to reduce long-term cost even after discontinuation of the one-time $1 billion contribution made in 2022/2023; and a 5 percent increase in the intermediate school district (ISD) operations allocation.

Looking forward, the May 2023 conference projected 2024, 2025, and 2026: a substantial 2023 surplus carries into 2024 but is significantly reduced by one-time payments, with 2025 projected to return to significant surplus. Risks flagged are inflation and a potential recession. Federal education-focused pandemic aid concludes September 30, 2024 — the "federal funding cliff." Planning factors listed include use of the ESSER III/11t allocation, staff retention and recruitment, student attraction and retention, pupil count trends, learning loss programming after pandemic funding ends, expanded GSRP preschool, food service redesign under the state free meal program, staffing and inflationary operating cost increases, technology costs, and school security and mental health staffing and costs. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference was scheduled for January 2024.

**Michigan School Meals**
Beginning in 2023/2024, free breakfast and lunch are available to all Michigan students under amendments to the State Aid Act, state funded for students who do not qualify under the National School Lunch and National School Breakfast programs. Participation is not automatic: districts must apply using the 2024 Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system. Eligibility requires being a public school, charter school, or ISD; participating in the National School Lunch Program; serving breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students; adopting the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) where the district qualifies; collecting family income information; and writing off all outstanding student negative balances. The Food Service Fund may not absorb that write-off, which requires funding from outside the fund under MDE guidance. Districts must track and claim meals as for federal programs and plan for higher participation across staffing, meal timing, cafeteria seating, menu planning, food orders, and family communications.

**MPSERS plan-level net liabilities**
The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2022 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $37.9 billion, an increase of approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022, up approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021. The primary driver in both cases was investment performance: a 27.2 percent annual return for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**Accounting and reporting changes ahead**
The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013; an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued in June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021, and Plante & Moran, PLLC submitted comments. The GASB's goal was final standards by March 2024. At its June 2023 meeting the GASB tentatively decided to remove all issues related to governmental fund reporting from the proposed statement's scope, which would significantly reduce its impact. Proposed changes had included additional MD&A information and a variance column in the budget-to-actual statement. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could change the timing of revenue and expense recognition; the GASB work plan anticipates issuance during 2027.

GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, requires recording a liability in the full accrual statements for leave attributable to services already rendered, that accumulates, and that is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the financial statement date. It removes the requirement to disclose gross additions and reductions (net change may be disclosed instead) and the requirement to disclose which funds liquidate the liability. It is effective for the School District's year ending June 30, 2025.

**Sinking fund and bond reporting**
Legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and maintenance equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, used to carry parts, equipment, and personnel for maintenance of school buildings. Sinking funds authorized (1) prior to March 29, 2017, (2) between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and (3) after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance. Prior allowable uses — real estate, buildings, building improvements, and technology — were not amended. A district levying a sinking fund must have an annual independent audit of the fund including review of its uses.

During fiscal 2023/2024 the Michigan Department of Treasury will release Numbered Letter 2023-1, superseding Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4, effective for sinking fund and bond compliance audits required for the June 30, 2024 reporting period. Changes: districts will no longer submit financial information to Treasury upon bond closeout (Treasury will use audited statements already filed with the Department of Education) but must submit an annual transmittal letter reporting the status of the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is simplified to the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multi-series bonds approved by electors at the same time may have closeout reporting at the end of the final issue without Treasury approval; and sinking fund levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a capital projects fund separate from remaining balances from pre-May 7, 2023 levies, potentially requiring a new separate fund.

**Arbitrage, cybersecurity, and real estate**
Arbitrage — the difference between interest paid by the bond issuer and earnings on invested bond proceeds — has drawn attention amid rising interest rates. As a tax-exempt entity the district is subject to federal arbitrage rules limiting retained earnings, should work with its bond advisor on recurring computations, generally performs a computation at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale to report excess earnings to the Internal Revenue Service, and uses the annual calculations to determine whether to report an arbitrage liability at June 30 in the full accrual statements.

On data security, the letter notes education remains a top ransomware target and cites the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021, signed into law in October 2021. It observes that the human element is the weakest link (passwords such as "August2023" are easily guessed) and asks whether staff are aware of phishing, whether data with personally identifiable information or FERPA-covered data sits on file-sharing sites, flash drives, or personal email accounts, and how secure data is with remote work; an external vulnerability assessment is suggested.

Understanding that the School District is considering how to leverage or better utilize real estate assets, the firm recommends evaluating options — demolishing and rebuilding, redeveloping for alternative purposes, leasing the building or land, or selling — and offers an introduction to its affiliated real estate consulting entity, Plante Moran Cresa.

2023_22_troy_school_district_0623_single.paragraph: Troy School District's draft Federal Awards Supplemental Information for the year ended June 30, 2023 — the single audit package prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC with auditor's reports dated October 6, 2023 — reports $13,844,823 of federal expenditures against $39,076,556 in award amounts (memo only). Unmodified compliance opinions were issued on all three major programs: the Child Nutrition Cluster, the Education Stabilization Fund, and the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act Cluster. No material weaknesses or significant deficiencies were identified, no current-year findings were reported, and the district qualified as a low-risk auditee at a $750,000 type A/type B threshold.

**What it is**
Draft "Federal Awards Supplemental Information, June 30, 2023" for Troy School District, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC. **Summary of auditor's results**

Total accrued revenue was $6,419,392 at July 1, 2022 and $5,147,518 at June 30, 2023; payments/in-kind received totaled $15,116,697; prior year expenditures totaled $20,321,267; adjustments and transfers and cash transferred to subrecipients were both zero.

**Largest individual programs**
ESSER III Section 11t Equalization (project 213723, 84.425U) is the single largest, with an $11,536,194 award and $4,828,798 of current-year expenditures, leaving $3,754,755 accrued at June 30, 2023. Total Education Stabilization Fund expenditures were $5,650,719 on $15,459,865 of awards. Other sizable items: National School Lunch Program - 23 ($1,233,538 expended), National Lunch Program Commodities - 23 ($686,811), Supply Chain Assistance ($555,904), IDEA Flowthrough 2223 ($2,360,178), Title III English Learners ($250,532 total), Total Adult Education ($375,589), Total Title I, Part A ($233,797), and Total TANF ($219,950).

**Reconciliation and notes**
Revenue from federal sources reported on the financial statements across all funds was $16,849,413; deducting $3,004,590 of MDE Child Care Stabilization Fund beneficiary payments not subject to single audit yields the $13,844,823 of federal expenditures per the SEFA. The notes state the Schedule follows 2 CFR Part 200; negative amounts represent adjustments or credits to prior-year reported expenditures; the School District elected not to use the 10 percent de minimis indirect cost rate; management used the Michigan Department of Education NexSys Grant Auditor Report (GAR) in preparing the Schedule, with differences relating to payment timing; and noncash assistance was valued per the Uniform Guidance.

**Scope and reports**
Draft "Troy School District — Federal Awards Supplemental Information, June 30, 2023," prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC and marked Draft throughout. It contains: the Report on the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Required by the Uniform Guidance (page 1); the Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance with Government Auditing Standards (page 2); the Report on Compliance for Each Major Federal Program and Report on Internal Control Over Compliance Required by the Uniform Guidance (pages 3-4); the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (pages 5-8); the Reconciliation of Basic Financial Statements Federal Revenue with the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (page 9); Notes to the Schedule (page 10); and the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs (page 11).

The auditors audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023, issuing their report dated October 6, 2023 containing unmodified opinions; no procedures were performed on the audited financial statements after October 6, 2023. All three reports in this package are dated October 6, 2023. The auditors opined that the schedule of expenditures of federal awards and the reconciliation are fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole. Under Government Auditing Standards they identified no deficiencies in internal control considered to be material weaknesses, and tests of compliance disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters required to be reported. On major program compliance they concluded that the School District complied, in all material respects, with the compliance requirements identified in the OMB Compliance Supplement that could have a direct and material effect on each major federal program for the year ended June 30, 2023, and identified no deficiencies in internal control over compliance considered to be material weaknesses. Audits were conducted under GAAS, Government Auditing Standards, and Title 2 U.S. Code of Federal Regulations Part 200 (Uniform Guidance).
